segments.title: The Fog and the Law: Opening the Chancery

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close, unhurried look at one of the great novels of the English language.
Over this series, we'll be moving through Dickens chapter by chapter — through the fog, through the courts, through the lives of people caught in the machinery of a system that feeds on them.
Today we begin at the beginning — the famous opening pages, with their fog and mud and the Lord Chancellor sitting in Lincoln's Inn Hall.
I'm joined by three guests whose company I'm very glad of for this journey.

Oliver Trevelyan has voiced more classic novels in audiobook form than perhaps anyone alive — he comes to Dickens as a performer, hearing the prose as something written for the voice first and the page second.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who reads every novel as a story about individual character — about goodness, self-sacrifice, the will tested by circumstance.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with Bleak House since she first read it as a teenager — she brings the experience of a devoted re-reader, alive to the verbal music.
Edmund, let's start with you — because the opening of this novel is one of the most audacious things Dickens ever did.
It is, and I think the audacity is often misread.
People reach for the word 'symbolic' almost immediately — the fog stands for the law, the mud stands for corruption, and so on.
But before it is symbolic of anything, it is a piece of prose written with extraordinary physical precision.
Consider what Dickens does in the very first sentences — no verbs, almost no grammar, just nouns and weather accumulating like the mud itself.
And then, without warning, he gives us this:

"As much mud in the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus, forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn Hill."
An extinct creature, walking through the streets of London as if perfectly at home.
That is not a political metaphor — that is a novelist trusting the sheer strangeness of the world he is rendering.
Edmund is right that it's physical — but I'd say it's also deeply, gloriously theatrical.
When I first read those opening pages aloud in the recording booth, I realised that Dickens has written stage directions.
'London. Michaelmas term lately over.' — those are not sentences, they're lighting cues.
And the Megalosaurus — Edmund, that word doesn't just arrive, it lumbers in.
The comedy of 'waddling like an elephantine lizard' is pitch-perfect — two syllables, then five, then the hill.
Dickens knows exactly how many syllables it takes to make something funny.
What strikes me, reading it again now, is the line about the sun.
The smoke makes 'a soft black drizzle, with flakes of soot in it as big as full-grown snowflakes — gone into mourning, one might imagine, for the death of the sun.'
That parenthetical — 'one might imagine' — is doing something very subtle.
It's the narrator half-apologising for his own extravagance, then refusing the apology entirely.
And 'the death of the sun' — three words that in any other context would seem overwrought — here feel completely earned.
I want to resist slightly the idea that this opening is primarily about the law.
The fog descends upon everyone — the foot passengers jostling umbrellas, the horses splashed to their blinkers.
Dickens is drawing a picture of human life as such — prone to confusion, to slipping, to ill temper.
The Chancery is one institution caught in that fog — but it is not the fog itself.
That's a generous reading of the Court of Chancery, Edmund.
Dickens, rather brilliantly, gives us his own view of the law's purpose a few hundred pages later — and he's not in a forgiving mood.
He writes, quite directly:
"The one great principle of the English law is to make business for itself."
Not a metaphor, not an atmosphere — a statement.
And then he twists the knife: 'surely they will cease to grumble' — the most perfectly placed mock-reassurance in Victorian fiction.
Oliver, you've made me think of the Smallweeds — because they feel like a living answer to that question of what the law's logic produces in human beings.
There's a passage about their family history that is one of the strangest and funniest things in the book.
The house of Smallweed has 'discarded all amusements, discountenanced all story-books, fairy-tales, fictions, and fables, and banished all levities whatsoever.'
Every generation going out early, marrying late — the whole family tree bent by the same commercial gravity.
And what does that produce?
Children who are not children at all.
Caroline has found the best sentence in the Smallweed chapter — let me read it properly, because it's a miniature masterpiece of disgust.

"Hence the gratifying fact that it has had no child born to it and that the complete little men and women whom it has produced have been observed to bear a likeness to old monkeys with something depressing on their minds."
'The gratifying fact.' That word 'gratifying' — Dickens is purring with righteous contempt.
And 'old monkeys with something depressing on their minds' — I defy anyone to read that aloud without the slightest flicker of delight.
The comedy is undeniable — but I'd note that what Dickens is attacking is the extirpation of the imagination.
Story-books, fairy-tales, fictions, fables — those aren't frivolities to Dickens, they are the things that make us human.
A family that has banished all that has banished the moral imagination itself — and that, I think, is his deepest charge against the world of Chancery and commerce alike.
And that's a thread we'll be pulling throughout this series — what it costs to live inside this system, and what it costs those who built it.

There's a moment — and Oliver, I want to bring you to this — where the narrator turns that gothic atmosphere toward something very specific: two people watching each other, and the stars watching them both.
A passage that introduces the idea of fate in this novel — of an ending already written somewhere in the dark.
It's a passage I find genuinely unnerving — and Dickens writes very little that is genuinely unnerving without also being very beautiful.
Tulkinghorn and Lady Dedlock have been circling each other — a cold war of secrets and surveillance.
And then the narrator pulls back, into the moonlight, into a kind of prophecy:
"Where are the digger and the spade, this peaceful night, destined to add the last great secret to the many secrets of the Tulkinghorn existence?"
'Is the man born yet, is the spade wrought yet?'
Someone will dig Tulkinghorn's grave — and Dickens is asking us whether that person exists yet, as we read.
That is the narrator as fate itself — which is a very different thing from social critique.
And it connects, doesn't it, to the passage about Lady Dedlock much later — when everything the fog seemed to promise has finally fallen.
I find those three words — 'So! All is broken down' — almost unbearable to read.
The narrator gives us her situation in one terrible sentence:
"Her name is in these many mouths, her husband knows his wrongs, her shame will be published — may be spreading while she thinks about it."
'May be spreading while she thinks about it' — that present tense, that simultaneity — is devastating.
Everything the fog at the beginning seemed to hold in suspension has broken open.
Caroline puts her finger on something essential about how Dickens structures this novel.
The atmosphere of the opening is not decorative — it is prophetic.
What the fog obscures at the beginning, the plot will eventually illuminate — at great cost to those inside it.
And the moral weight of those revelations falls not on institutions but on persons — on a woman with a secret, and a man who kept it over her like a weapon.
Fog as prophecy — I think that's a phrase we'll return to more than once.
We've set the stage — the mud, the court, the watching stars, and the families shaped by a world that has discarded all levities whatsoever.
In our next segment, we'll be moving deeper into the novel's double narrative — and into the voice of Esther Summerson, who sees all of this from the inside.

segments.title: The Comic Gallery: Grotesques and Performers

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
I'm joined today by three exceptional readers of Dickens, each of whom brings a very different set of instincts to the page.
Oliver Trevelyan has given voice to more classic novels than perhaps any living reader — he hears this prose the way a musician hears a score.
Sir Edmund Leigh brings the moral rigour of a lifetime's scholarship — and a very healthy suspicion of anyone who reduces great fiction to a political argument.
And Caroline Woodcourt is one of our finest book critics — someone who came to this novel as a teenager and has never quite left it.
Today we're in Chapter Thirteen — the scene where Richard and Ada confide their love to Esther, and Mr. Jarndyce steps in with counsel that is tender, wise, and quietly ominous.
What I love about this scene is that Dickens gives us the very mechanism of his own narrative art.
Esther sits between Richard and Ada — literally flanked by the young lovers — and she says something that stops you cold.
She says:
"They went on in their own wild way for a little while — I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself."
That parenthetical — 'I enjoyed it too much myself' — that is Esther's entire secret inner life in eight words.
She presents herself as the sensible one, the governess-figure — and then she slips up and tells you she's as romantic as either of them.
And that admission makes her counsel so much more affecting when it comes.
She doesn't simply wish them well and send them off.
She sets conditions — real conditions about constancy and duty and fortitude.
The passage reads:

"it could come to happiness only if it were real and lasting and inspired them with a steady resolution to do their duty to each other, with constancy, fortitude, and perseverance, each always for the other's sake."
Three words in a row — constancy, fortitude, perseverance.
They sound like the virtues on a family coat of arms — and in a way, that's exactly what they are for Esther.
One hears, of course, the cadences of a very old tradition — the sermon, the homily, the grave address to the young.
But what distinguishes Dickens here is that the gravity is entirely earned by character.
It is Esther speaking — a young woman who has known privation and joylessness from the very beginning of her life.
When she speaks of constancy and duty, she speaks from experience, not prescription.
And then Jarndyce arrives — and the novel shifts register entirely.
Jarndyce is one of Dickens's supreme achievements in the mode of the benevolent eccentric — and yet he consistently outflanks that category.
Listen to how he handles the possibility that Richard and Ada may simply fall out of love.
"I will assume that a few years hence you will be in your hearts to one another what you are to-day."
He assumes the best.
But then — immediately — he provides for the worst.
"if you DO come to find that you are more commonplace cousins to each other as man and woman than you were as boy and girl — don't be ashamed still to confide in me."
That word — commonplace.
It's the most quietly devastating word in the passage — and Jarndyce uses it with perfect tenderness.
What moves me is the small joke he allows himself — 'your manhood will excuse me, Rick!'
It's an acknowledgement of Richard's pride — the masculine vanity that may bristle at the suggestion love could diminish.
Jarndyce disarms it with a light touch, and moves straight on.
And then comes the great speech about effort — which I think is the moral spine of the whole chapter.
"Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts.
Never separate the two, like the heathen waggoner."
The heathen waggoner — who prays for his cart to move but does not push it.
It's the perfect compressed parable for Richard's entire future trajectory.
Precisely — and here I think Dickens is at his most genuinely serious as a moralist.
This is not satire.
This is a direct statement about the relationship between will and outcome — about what it means to mean something.
The passage says it plainly:
"If you had the abilities of all the great men, past and present, you could do nothing well without sincerely meaning it and setting about it."
Ability without sincere application — that is Richard Carstone's tragedy in eight chapters' time, announced here with perfect clarity.
Dickens is not being sentimental.
And we get a very precise clinical reading of that deficiency from a marvellous minor character — Mrs. Badger.
A woman who is primarily distinguished, in the novel's accounting, by her two spectacularly accomplished late husbands.
But she delivers, in the driest possible fashion, the most accurate diagnosis of Richard's problem.
She tells Esther:
"He has not that positive interest in it which makes it his vocation.
If he has any decided impression in reference to it, I should say it was that it is a tiresome pursuit."
A tiresome pursuit.
In two words, the medical profession is dispensed with — and so, effectively, is Richard.
What Mrs. Badger understands — and what makes this such a cutting contrast — is that true vocation looks nothing like Richard.
She holds up Allan Woodcourt as the counter-example.

"Young men like Mr. Allan Woodcourt who take it from a strong interest in all that it can do will find some reward in it through a great deal of work for a very little money and through years of considerable endurance and disappointment."
A great deal of work for a very little money — and Dickens presents that as the noble condition.
The reward is in the commitment itself, not in the outcome.
One ought to note that Woodcourt is not simply a moral foil — he is a fully realised portrait of what Dickens genuinely admired in a human being.
A man of no great fortune, no connections, no inheritance — but formed entirely by what he sincerely means to do.
That is the Johnsonian ideal — that character is constituted by habitual action, not by feeling or intention.
Richard, by contrast, has abundance of feeling and a great vacancy of habitual effort.
And we feel all of that — the promise and the portent — in the most luminous piece of writing in this chapter.
When Ada and Richard leave, Esther watches them pass through the sunlit rooms.
And she writes:

"So young, so beautiful, so full of hope and promise, they went on lightly through the sunlight as their own happy thoughts might then be traversing the years to come and making them all years of brightness.
So they passed away into the shadow and were gone.
It was only a burst of light that had been so radiant.
The room darkened as they went out, and the sun was clouded over."
You can't improve on that.
The repetition of 'So' — 'So young,' 'So they passed' — it has the rhythm of a lament already.
We are watching a funeral, in a way, before the life has been lived.
'The room darkened as they went out' — the novel is telling us everything we need to know about Richard Carstone in one physical fact.
It is, at bottom, a deeply moral image.
Dickens does not say Richard is doomed by society or by circumstance.
He says the light changes when Richard leaves — and we understand, because we have watched his character, precisely why.
Three readers, one scene — and between you, I think you've shown us how much Dickens packs into what might look, at first glance, like a simple domestic interlude.
Jarndyce's counsel, Esther's tender watchfulness, Mrs. Badger's diagnosis — and that closing image of the sunlight failing.
In our next segment, we'll be turning to some of Dickens's great comic grotesques — the characters who exist almost as forces of nature rather than people.
Do stay with us.

segments.title: Richard's Slow Dissolution: Ambition and Ruin

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We turn now to one of the novel's most quietly devastating arcs — the slow ruin of Richard Carstone.
Richard begins the novel as a charming, gifted young man with every advantage — and ends it broken by a lawsuit that was never really about money at all.
With us to unpick what Dickens is doing here are our three guests.
Oliver Trevelyan, who has voiced more Dickens audiobooks than any living person and reads this novel as a performer first.
Sir Edmund Leigh, the retired Oxford don who believes great novels are finally about character tested by circumstance — not social programme.
And Caroline Woodcourt, critic and devoted re-reader of this novel, who cares above all about what the text actually does to you on the page.

Edmund, let's start with you — Richard's dissolution is inseparable from the world around him, and there's a passage early in the novel about Lady Dedlock and the machinery of fashionable society that I think illuminates something about how people get managed without knowing it.
Yes, and one must be careful not to overreach with such a passage — it is satire of fashion, not a thesis about determinism.
And yet what Dickens establishes here is deeply relevant to Richard.
The passage describes Lady Dedlock's conviction that she is an inscrutable being — quite out of reach of ordinary mortals.
And yet every dim little star revolving about her knows her weaknesses and caprices — and nurses her accordingly.
The jewellers, the mercers, the librarian — each one says, in effect: know where to have your people, and you can turn them round your finger.
Dickens gives us this magnificent image — and I want to read it precisely as he wrote it.
"who, in hooking one, hook all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet of the majestic Lilliput"
The comedy is real — the Gulliver allusion is perfectly placed — but the point beneath it is serious.
Richard believes he controls his own choices — the Chancery suit, the army, the law — but he is being led, flattered, and hooked, no less than Lady Dedlock by her tradespeople.
That Gulliver comparison is one of Dickens's great comic strokes — and Edmund is right that it carries genuine weight.
When you read it aloud — and I have, many times — the rhythm of it is almost gleeful.
Dickens is enjoying himself enormously even as he's anatomising something quite pitiless.
And with Richard, the tragedy is that he lacks even the grandeur of Lady Dedlock's self-delusion.
She imagines herself inscrutable and magnificent — and she is, at least, magnificent.
Richard imagines he is about to be vindicated by a lawsuit — and he is simply dying.
What strikes me is how tenderly Dickens holds Richard, even as he's showing us the mechanism of his ruin.
There's a passage in chapter fifty-one that I keep returning to — Ada's gesture.
Esther watches as Ada rises, and the description Dickens gives is almost impossibly beautiful.
"my darling rose, put off her bonnet, kneeled down beside him with her golden hair falling like sunlight on his head, clasped her two arms round his neck, and turned her face to me"
He is meditative, looking at the ground — already half-absent from the world.
And Ada pours herself over him like light.
It's one of those moments where you simply have to stop reading and breathe.
Caroline is right to slow down there — that image is doing a great deal of work.
The golden hair falling like sunlight — this is not mere prettiness.
It is the last benediction of innocence over a man who has chosen, freely, to destroy himself.
That is where I part company with readings that would make Richard merely a victim of the Chancery system.
He has a will — he exercises it badly — and Ada's love cannot save what he will not save himself.
And yet Ada does not stop hoping — which is what makes her genuinely heroic in a novel full of capable women.
There's a passage late in the novel where Ada describes what she imagines for her unborn child — and it is heartbreaking precisely because it is so full of life.
She says — and this is Ada speaking to Esther — she looks forward to the future through years and years.

"Or that a generous brave man, as handsome as he used to be, as hopeful, and far more happy, may walk in the sunshine with him, honouring his grey head and saying to himself, 'I thank God this is my father! Ruined by a fatal inheritance, and restored through me!'"
Ruined by a fatal inheritance, and restored through me — that phrase is carrying the whole novel's argument on its back.
Ada imagines a son doing for his father what the father could not do for himself.
She is grieving, and she is hoping, at the same moment — and Dickens gives her the language for both.
That vision Ada conjures — the son in sunshine, the grey-haired father — it undoes me every time.
But what Dickens knows, and what we know as readers by that point, is that Richard will not live to grey hair.
So Ada's hope is already an elegy.
And there's a parallel image earlier — one that haunts the whole novel — from Esther's narration.
Very early in the book, Esther covers a dead baby with her handkerchief — and she writes this, years later, looking back.

"How little I thought, when I raised my handkerchief to look upon the tiny sleeper underneath and seemed to see a halo shine around the child through Ada's drooping hair as her pity bent her head — how little I thought in whose unquiet bosom that handkerchief would come to lie after covering the motionless and peaceful breast!"
The halo around the child, Ada's drooping hair — we've already been shown this iconography of devotion and loss.
Dickens plants the image of Ada bending over a body in pity so early — and then redeems it, or rather repeats it, in chapter fifty-one.
Caroline has identified something crucial there — the structural rhyming of images across the novel's great length.
And the Thames passage — Esther and Bucket crossing the river in search of her mother — extends the same pattern into pure gothic atmosphere.
Esther writes of it years afterward, and it has not left her.

"The river had a fearful look, so overcast and secret, creeping away so fast between the low flat lines of shore — so heavy with indistinct and awful shapes, both of substance and shadow; so death-like and mysterious."
Overcast and secret — creeping — death-like.
The prose is doing what Dickens's prose does at its highest — making the external world confess the interior one.
Esther says she has seen the river many times since — by sunlight, by moonlight — but never free from those impressions.
That is not allegory — that is how grief and fear actually work on a human mind.
Edmund is being gracious there — because that is also a profoundly political image of the Thames, whether he'll admit it or not.
But I take his point — Dickens earns it at the level of character first.
What strikes me, reading the river passage aloud, is the weight of those triplets — overcast and secret, substance and shadow, death-like and mysterious.
Dickens is a musician when he wants to be — and that passage wants to be read slowly, almost held in the mouth.
The lights on the bridge always burning dim, the cutting wind, the pale carriage-lamp reflected back — and then: a face rising out of the dreaded water.
There is no finer sentence of dread in the whole novel — and this novel is not short of competitors.

What comes through in all three of these passages is how Dickens weaves the fates of his characters together — the dead child, the dark river, Ada kneeling in the light, the unborn son who may one day redeem his father.
Richard's dissolution is never just his own story — it's refracted through every person who loved him.
In our next segment, we'll look more closely at the institution at the heart of that ruin — Chancery itself, and what Dickens makes of it.

segments.title: A Woman's Secret: Lady Dedlock and Narrative Machinery

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great novel apart and holds each piece up to the light.
Today's segment sits at the cold heart of the novel: the story of Lady Dedlock and the secret that will destroy her.
Joining me, as ever, are our three guests.
Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and narrator of more classic novels than any living voice — brings his performer's ear to the rhythms and timing of Dickens's prose.
Sir Edmund Leigh, retired Oxford don, reads Dickens as a moralist — interested above all in character tested by circumstance.
And Caroline Woodcourt, book critic and devoted re-reader of this novel, who attends always to what the prose does on the pulse.
The question before us: how does Dickens build the machinery of Lady Dedlock's secret — and what does it cost her to carry it?
What strikes me first, every time, is the sheer theatrical craft of how the secret is announced.
Sir Leicester reads out Tulkinghorn's letter — slowly, fumblingly, with the eye-glass, with the wrong paragraph first.
Dickens makes us wait for the line just as Lady Dedlock has to wait.
And when it comes, it is so matter-of-fact it lands like a stone dropped into still water.
Tulkinghorn writes, and Sir Leicester reads aloud:
"I have something to tell her on her return in reference to the person who copied the affidavit in the Chancery suit, which so powerfully stimulated her curiosity. I have seen him."
Three words. "I have seen him." That's the whole detonation.
And Dickens gives it to us through the most oblivious possible mouth — Sir Leicester, who understands absolutely nothing of what he's just said.
That comic misdirection of Sir Leicester with the eye-glass and the wrong paragraph — it's almost unbearable, isn't it.
We're reading it from the outside, but we feel Lady Dedlock's impatience as if it were our own.
Dickens even notes — she "looks a little irritated."
A little irritated. That is all the novel permits her, in public.
And that is Dickens's whole method with her — tiny cracks in the composure, just enough to let us see the pressure within.
The secret doesn't live in what she says. It lives in what she cannot afford to show.
What Caroline identifies is, I think, the moral centre of the character.
Lady Dedlock is not merely concealing a piece of information. She is performing a self that she has constructed over many years.
And the exhaustion of that performance — the word Dickens returns to again and again — is the real subject.
He calls her, magnificently, an "exhausted deity, surrounded by worshippers, and terribly liable to be bored to death, even while presiding at her own shrine."
The word "terribly" is doing quiet work there. This is not social ennui. This is existential dread wearing the costume of ennui.
She has made herself into a performance so convincing that even she is trapped by it.
Edmund puts his finger on something I feel acutely as a performer.
"Speechless repository of noble confidences" — that's Tulkinghorn.
"So oddly out of place and yet so perfectly at home."
It's the most chilling description of a lawyer in all of English fiction, and it's done in one clause.
The two of them together in a room — it's like watching two chess players who've agreed never to touch a piece.
And Dickens makes the tension between them almost architectural — built into the very grammar of the prose.
That long passage in the parallel construction — "whether each evermore watches and suspects the other..." — it goes on and on, clause by clause, neither resolution nor rest.
Let me read it, because you really have to hear the accumulation of it:

"Whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares; what each would give to know how much the other knows — all this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts."
"For the time." Those three words at the end are the whole dread of the novel compressed into a subordinate clause.
It won't be hidden forever. Dickens tells you that in the very sentence that pretends to withhold.
The secret, of course, has its other dimension — Esther herself, who does not yet know she is the secret.
Mr. Jarndyce's account of what was told to him is extraordinarily careful — and the care itself is eloquent.
He was told by a woman who would not give her real name:

"That she was, if there were any ties of blood in such a case, the child's aunt. That more than this she would never — and he was well persuaded of the steadfastness of her resolution — for any human consideration disclose."
"The steadfastness of her resolution." Kenge believed it. Jarndyce believed it. And so do we.
This is a woman who has made secrecy not merely a decision but a discipline — a form of moral self-government, however misguided we might think it.
One might even say — and here I suspect I part company from certain fashionable readings — that there is something admirable in the sheer will of it.
I take Edmund's point, and I'd push it a little further in a different direction.
Because the secret doesn't only belong to Lady Dedlock. It radiates outward and begins to bend other characters.
Richard Carstone, for instance — he has his own affliction, which is almost a mirror image: not the secret of the past but the delusion about the future.
He says to Esther — heartbreakingly, because he's trying so hard to be honest about himself:

"I wish to heaven I were a more constant sort of fellow... If I were a more constant sort of fellow, I should have held on either to Badger or to Kenge and Carboy like grim death, and should have begun to be steady and systematic by this time, and shouldn't be in debt."
Lady Dedlock knows too much. Richard knows too little about himself. Chancery is the machine that keeps both of them in its grip.
That's a beautiful pairing, Oliver — the secret and the self-deception as twin modes of being trapped.
Richard's sentence trails off, doesn't it — "and shouldn't be in debt, and—" That dash is everything.
He can't finish the sentence because he doesn't know what the end of it looks like.
Lady Dedlock knows exactly how her sentence ends — and that knowledge is its own form of imprisonment.
The secret that imprisons, the delusion that consumes — and Tulkinghorn holding the keys to both.
We'll be returning to all three of these threads as the season continues.
Oliver Trevelyan, Sir Edmund Leigh, Caroline Woodcourt — thank you for a remarkable conversation.
Next time on Bleak House Unpacked, we turn to the fog — not just as weather, but as the novel's first and most persistent argument.

segments.title: The Crossing Sweep: Social Suffering and Dickens's Conscience

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the programme that takes Dickens's great fog-bound novel apart, chapter by chapter, to see what makes it endure.
I'm joined today by three guests whose combined knowledge of this novel would fill a small library — and whose disagreements fill the room rather pleasantly.
Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and narrator of more classic audiobooks than any living person — hears every sentence as a performance waiting to happen.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who insists that great fiction is about individual moral life, not social programme — and who says so with enviable precision.
And Caroline Woodcourt — book critic and lifelong reader of Victorian fiction — cares above all about what a sentence does to you when you read it alone at midnight.
Today we're looking at a stark contrast that sits near the heart of the novel — the warmth of Bleak House itself, and the desolation of Jo, the crossing-sweep.
Before we get to the wretchedness — and there is magnificent wretchedness ahead — I want to dwell for a moment on those first impressions of Bleak House itself.
Because Dickens has Esther describe a house where everything is pleasantly irregular — odd portraits in the wrong rooms, angels carrying a complacent gentleman to heaven in festoons.
It's comic, it's tender, and it sets up the whole moral architecture of what Jarndyce's home means in this novel.
And then Dickens pulls it all together in one great cumulative sentence that Esther speaks as if she can barely believe her luck.
"with its light, and warmth, and comfort; with its hospitable jingle, at a distance, of preparations for dinner; with the face of its generous master brightening everything we saw"
That word, hospitable jingle — you can hear it.
Dickens writes for the ear first, always.
Oliver is quite right about the acoustic quality of that sentence, and I wouldn't undervalue it.
But what strikes me about that passage is the moral fact it establishes — that Jarndyce's generosity literally illuminates the house.
The face of its generous master brightening everything we saw — character, not circumstance, is what makes a place habitable.
Dickens believed that profoundly, whatever the social critics wish to make of him.
What I love about that room description is the quirkiness Dickens allows Esther to notice — the trout staring back at portraits of surprised birds.
Esther is allowed to find things funny, which she doesn't always get credit for.
And yet the cumulative sentence at the end tips into something genuinely tender — rose-leaves and sweet lavender stored in every possible drawer.
That detail carries the whole promise of the house — that nothing will be wasted, nothing overlooked.
And that promise, of course, is precisely what the world outside the house refuses to extend to a great many of its inhabitants.
Which brings us to Jo — and to one of the most devastating passages in the entire novel.
The passage in which Jo gives his testimony at the inquest is, in my view, the moment Dickens is at his most purely moral.
I say moral deliberately — not political, not polemical.
Dickens strips this child down to almost nothing — and in the stripping, reveals what cannot be taken away.
The passage reads like a litany of negatives, and then it turns.
"No father, no mother, no friends. Never been to school."
And yet — he knows a broom is a broom, and he knows it is wicked to tell a lie.
That is not merely pathos. That is Dickens insisting on the inalienable moral core of a human being.
When I've read that passage aloud — and I have, many times — there is always a moment of silence in the room after those two sentences.
No father, no mother, no friends. You cannot dress that up. You just have to let it land.
What Dickens is doing technically is using the free-indirect style of the omniscient narrator to inhabit Jo's own register — short, blunt, declarative.
The narrator doesn't pity from above. He thinks in Jo's own rhythms.
That, Edmund, is also a form of moral imagination — and a formal one.
I grant that entirely. The formal choice is inseparable from the moral intention — which is precisely my point.
Dickens is not writing a pamphlet. He is writing a soul.
And then the narrator speaks directly to Jo — one of those moments where Dickens simply breaks the frame and addresses the character himself.
Jo, is it thou — that sudden shift into a biblical register, almost a benediction.
And then Dickens finds Jo's one fragment of light, and he reads it with such care.
"There is something like a distant ray of light in thy muttered reason for this: 'He wos wery good to me, he wos!'"
A distant ray. Not salvation, not vindication — just one act of remembered kindness.
And Dickens says that is enough. That is sufficient to keep Jo out of outer darkness.
That phonetic spelling — wery good to me, he wos — is doing so much work.
It signals the limits of Jo's language without condescending to them — the emotion is vast, and the words are few.
The contrast with Mrs. Piper's testimony in the same chapter is almost comic in its ferocity.
Mrs. Piper has an enormous amount to say — chiefly in parentheses and without punctuation — and almost nothing to tell.
Whereas Jo's testimony fits on three lines and contains a complete moral universe.
Mrs. Piper is the novel's great accidental satirist — she testifies at length and illuminates nothing except her own confusion.
But before we leave the world of suffering outside the gates, there's a passage involving two brick-maker's wives that I'd like to turn to.
Jenny's speech about her dead child is the one that undoes me every time I read it.
It's so simply put. And yet structurally it's this extraordinary loop — death generating love generating fear of loss.
She says — and I have to read this exactly as Dickens wrote it —
"It's my dead child that makes me love this child so dear, and it's my dead child that makes her love it so dear too"
"we mean the same thing, if we knew how to say it, us two mothers does in our poor hearts!"
If we knew how to say it. That conditional breaks your heart.
These women are not inarticulate — they are reaching for something language barely contains.
What strikes me is the solidarity between the two women — and how naturally it arises from shared loss rather than from any doctrine.
Us two mothers does — that grammatical irregularity is not a sign of ignorance. It is an intensifier.
The we — the collective — is expressed in the only grammar available to them, and it is no less real for that.
Dickens understood that feeling precedes articulation, and that the distance between the two is itself a form of suffering.
When I read passages like Jenny's aloud, I always slow almost to a stop on that final phrase — in our poor hearts.
The adjective poor is doing triple duty there — poverty, modesty, tenderness.
And the exclamation mark at the end — which readers sometimes miss — that's not melodrama. That's the pressure of feeling escaping through syntax.
Dickens earned that exclamation mark.
Warmth in the drawing room of Bleak House, and grief in a brickmaker's cottage — Dickens holds both without flinching.
That, perhaps, is the novel's deepest structural argument — that the good home over there and the desolation over here are not separate worlds but one.
We'll pursue that argument further in our next segment. Thank you all.

segments.title: Voices and Rhythms: The Music of Dickens's Prose

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've been talking about the fog, the fog of Chancery, the fog of language.
But this segment is about something different: the sheer music of how Dickens writes.
The rhythms, the comic timing, the moments where the prose itself becomes the argument.
Oliver Trevelyan has been waiting for this conversation his entire career.
Over to you, Oliver.
Thank you, and yes — this is the conversation I most wanted to have.
Because Dickens is, above all things, a writer for the voice.
He performed his own work publicly for decades, to enormous audiences, and that performance instinct is baked into every sentence he wrote.
Let me start with Boythorn — because Boythorn is pure music.
This is a man who speaks in volleys.
Dickens tells us, literally, that he fires another volley — and you feel the percussion of it in the prose.
Boythorn is haranguing Sir Leicester Dedlock over a right of way, and the language builds and builds until it explodes.
"He brings actions for trespass; I bring actions for trespass. He brings actions for assault and battery; I defend them and continue to assault and batter. Ha, ha, ha!"
That triple "ha" — that's not punctuation, that's a stage direction.
Dickens knows exactly how long you hold the laugh.
What strikes me about that passage is the symmetry — the perfect mirroring of the legal language.
"He brings actions; I bring actions" — it's almost a round, a musical round.
And Dickens uses that rhythm to make the law look utterly absurd.
Two men doing exactly the same thing to each other, endlessly — and calling it justice.
But I keep coming back to the Pardiggle boys, because that's where the comic rhythm does something different.
It's not expansive, it's compressed — these tiny, shrivelled, furious children.
Listen to this:
"We had never seen such dissatisfied children. It was not merely that they were weazened and shrivelled—though they were certainly that too—but they looked absolutely ferocious with discontent."
"Ferocious with discontent" — you can hear the double-take built into that phrase.
You almost read it twice before you believe it.
The comic gift is undeniable.
But I'd ask us to notice what that comic gift is in service of.
The Pardiggle children aren't funny as an end in themselves — they are an indictment of a certain kind of adult vanity.
A mother who has drained these boys of their pocket money for her charities has also drained them of their childhood.
The grotesque is always moral with Dickens.
And consider the Chesney Wold passage — because there the rhythm does something entirely different again.
That long rolling sentence about Sir Leicester among his ancestral portraits:
"Each of us was a passing reality here and left this coloured shadow of himself and melted into remembrance as dreamy as the distant voices of the rooks now lulling you to rest."
That is extraordinary prose — lulling and melancholy and beautiful.
And yet the irony is present too — we are being made to feel the beauty of something Dickens is also quietly mocking.
Edmund, you've put your finger on something I feel every time I read that passage aloud.
The sentence genuinely lulls you — and then you surface and realise Dickens has been laughing at Sir Leicester the entire time.
He makes you inhabit the grandeur before he punctures it.
There's a similar trick with Jarndyce — but warmer, much warmer.
The comedy there is in the repetition — the sheer accumulation of evasions.
Ada's mother goes to thank Jarndyce, and:
"he happened to see her through a window coming to the door, and immediately escaped by the back gate, and was not heard of for three months."
Three months!
The pause before that detail — you hear Dickens timing it perfectly.
And the rhythm of that whole passage is wonderful — the children wondering and wondering about what the house will be like.
Dickens writes, "All of which we wondered about, over and over again."
That repetition is the rhythm of childhood anticipation — it mimics the feeling, not just describes it.
That's what Dickens does that nobody else quite manages — he finds the prose rhythm that is the emotional experience.
And then he can do something completely different in the very next chapter — something like Mrs. Snagsby.
The Snagsby passage is where the comedy tips into something genuinely eerie.
Listen to how the prose itself becomes a kind of haunting:
"And henceforth he begins, go where he will, to be attended by another shadow than his own, hardly less constant than his own, hardly less quiet than his own."
The repetition of "his own" — three times — it's incantatory.
It feels like a curse being laid, syllable by syllable.
The Snagsby passage is one of the great instances of Dickens finding a style that perfectly matches his subject.
Mrs. Snagsby is not merely jealous — she has become a principle of surveillance.
And the prose enacts that principle — relentless, repetitive, inescapable.
The final clause — "bone of his bone, flesh of his flesh, shadow of his shadow" — is a biblical inversion.
Marriage language turned into something predatory.
That is not comedy — that is dark wit of the highest order.
Edmund is absolutely right — and that's what makes Dickens so extraordinary to perform.
The register shifts without warning.
You go from the gleeful percussion of Boythorn's "Ha, ha, ha!" to this creeping, ghostly repetition over Mrs. Snagsby.
And the reader — or the listener — has to follow him through every gear change.
That range is the genius.
Boythorn firing volleys, Jarndyce fleeing by the back gate, Mrs. Snagsby as gothic shadow — all from the same pen, the same novel.
What a range.
In our next segment, we turn to the characters who carry the novel's moral weight — the ones Dickens asks us to truly love.

segments.title: The Web Complete: Character, Fate, and Moral Imagination

utterances.text: We've spent this episode tracing the great threads of Bleak House — the fog, the court, the secrets, the suffering.
Now, in our closing segment, I want to ask something larger: what does the novel finally make of all this?
Is it a moral vision? A social indictment? A kind of dark providence working itself out?
Edmund, I want to begin with you — because no one here is more alert to what Dickens demands of individual conscience.
Thank you. The novel is, at its deepest level, a meditation on what happens when a family allows pride to become its governing principle.
We are told, in that extraordinary ghost-passage early in the novel, about the first Lady Dedlock — the crippled lady who cursed the house.
Dickens gives her a voice of absolute, terrible finality.
'I will die here where I have walked. And I will walk here, though I am in my grave.'
'I will walk here until the pride of this house is humbled. And when calamity or when disgrace is coming to it, let the Dedlocks listen for my step!'
That is not merely atmosphere. That is a moral law being stated in the form of a ghost story.
And the novel proceeds to demonstrate, with the patience of a great moralist, that the law holds.
Edmund is absolutely right about the curse — and what I love is that Dickens earns it theatrically.
The woman never complained, never spoke — and then in her final extremity, she speaks in prophecy.
The silence makes the speech devastating.
But the novel doesn't only deal in the gothic register, does it? It deals in the absurdly comic with equal ferocity.
Jarndyce's great rant about Wiglomeration — I've read it aloud a hundred times and it never loses its comic fury.
He says — and notice the rhythmic accumulation here —

'He is a ward in Chancery, my dear. Kenge and Carboy will have something to say about it; Master Somebody — a sort of ridiculous sexton, digging graves for the merits of causes in a back room at the end of Quality Court, Chancery Lane — will have something to say about it.'
A sexton digging graves for the merits of causes. That is one of the great comic images in the English novel.
What strikes me — reading that passage — is how the comedy and the tragedy feed the same indictment.
Wiglomeration isn't just funny — it destroys Richard Carstone.
And Jarndyce sees the danger far earlier than Richard does — perhaps from the very beginning.
There's that tender, painful moment when he speaks to Richard and Ada about the future he'd hoped for them.

'When I contemplated these relations between us four which have so brightened my life and so invested it with new interests and pleasures, I certainly did contemplate, afar off, the possibility of you and your pretty cousin here — don't be shy, Ada, don't be shy, my dear! — being in a mind to go through life together.'
'But that was afar off, Rick, afar off!'
That repetition — afar off, afar off — is heartbreaking. He knows the Chancery pit has already swallowed the boy.
Caroline's reading of that passage is exactly right, and it connects to what I find most morally serious in the novel.
Jarndyce watches, understands, and cannot save Richard — because Richard will not save himself.
The weakness is interior. The court is the occasion, not the cause.
Though I grant that the detective strand introduces a rather different moral register — one of urgency, action, rescue.
Bucket's great speech to Jarndyce — pleading for Esther's help in finding Lady Dedlock — is extraordinary for its pragmatic moral force.
He says, with that peculiar professional humanity of his —
'If I follow her alone, she, being in ignorance of what Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, has communicated to me, may be driven to desperation.'

'But if I follow her in company with a young lady, answering to the description of a young lady that she has a tenderness for — I ask no question, and I say no more than that — she will give me credit for being friendly.'
I ask no question, and I say no more than that. The tact of that man is almost as admirable as his intelligence.
Bucket is one of those characters where Dickens seems to be enjoying himself almost too much.
That speech has the rhythm of a man who thinks at speed — all those conditional clauses piling up, each one a manoeuvre.
He's a detective, yes, but in that moment he's also a moral advocate — arguing for the one action that might save a life.
And then, against all this darkness — the curse, the court, the chase across a frozen night — Dickens gives us this.
Esther and Jarndyce step out of a porch. Seven words.
'We went out of the porch and he showed me written over it, Bleak House.'
After everything — that. The name given back, transformed.
I've read that sentence so many times and it still stops me cold.
Because Bleak House — the first Bleak House, Jarndyce's house — is a place of welcome, of shelter, of improbable warmth.
And now there will be another — built for Esther, named for that same hope.
It's Dickens saying: bleak is not the last word. It never was.
On that I think we are in perfect agreement.
The curse is real, the fog is real, the court destroys — and yet goodness persists, and shelters those who can accept it.
That is the moral imagination of a very great novelist.
Edmund Leigh, Caroline Woodcourt, Oliver Trevelyan — it has been a genuine pleasure to think through this novel with you.
Bleak House remains, after all these readings, a book that refuses to be exhausted.
Its fog still rolls in. Its chancery still grinds. And its Bleak Houses still stand.
Thank you for listening to Bleak House Unpacked.

Has Mr. Tulkinghorn any idea of this himself? It may be so, or it may
not, but there is this remarkable circumstance to be noted in
everything associated with my Lady Dedlock as one of a class—as one
of the leaders and representatives of her little world. She supposes
herself to be an inscrutable Being, quite out of the reach and ken of
ordinary mortals—seeing herself in her glass, where indeed she looks

dressmaker takes of her physical proportions. Is a new dress, a new
custom, a new singer, a new dancer, a new form of jewellery, a new
dwarf or giant, a new chapel, a new anything, to be set up? There are
deferential people in a dozen callings whom my Lady Dedlock suspects
of nothing but prostration before her, who can tell you how to manage
her as if she were a baby, who do nothing but nurse her all their

lead her and her whole troop after them; who, in hooking one, hook
all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet

forward. I look forward a long while, through years and years, and

c57:p18.text:
We appeared to retrace the way we had come. Not that I had taken note
of any particular objects in my perturbed state of mind, but judging
from the general character of the streets. We called at another
office or station for a minute and crossed the river again. During
the whole of this time, and during the whole search, my companion,
wrapped up on the box, never relaxed in his vigilance a single
moment; but when we crossed the bridge he seemed, if possible, to be
more on the alert than before. He stood up to look over the parapet,
he alighted and went back after a shadowy female figure that flitted
past us, and he gazed into the profound black pit of water with a
face that made my heart die within me. The river had a fearful look,
so overcast and secret, creeping away so fast between the low flat
lines of shore—so heavy with indistinct and awful shapes, both of
substance and shadow; so death-like and mysterious. I have seen it
many times since then, by sunlight and by moonlight, but never free
from the impressions of that journey. In my memory the lights upon
the bridge are always burning dim, the cutting wind is eddying round
the homeless woman whom we pass, the monotonous wheels are whirling
on, and the light of the carriage-lamps reflected back looks palely
in upon me—a face rising out of the dreaded water.
c57:p18.summary: The crossing back over the Thames is narrated with haunting detail; Esther's memory of the dark river, Bucket's vigilant searching, and her dread are woven into a Gothic tableau that haunts her permanently.

Mr. Tulkinghorn does so with deference and holds it open while she
passes out. She passes close to him, with her usual fatigued manner
and insolent grace. They meet again at dinner—again, next
day—again, for many days in succession. Lady Dedlock is always the
same exhausted deity, surrounded by worshippers, and terribly liable
to be bored to death, even while presiding at her own shrine. Mr.
Tulkinghorn is always the same speechless repository of noble
confidences, so oddly out of place and yet so perfectly at home. They
appear to take as little note of one another as any two people
enclosed within the same walls could. But whether each evermore
watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great
reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the
other, and never to be taken unawares; what each would give to know
how much the other knows—all this is hidden, for the time, in their
own hearts.

We walked a little way without speaking, and presently Richard
addressed me in his frankest and most feeling manner, thus: “My dear
Esther, I understand you, and I wish to heaven I were a more constant

(Somehow, I mean something that I can’t very well express, but you’ll
make it out.) If I were a more constant sort of fellow, I should have
held on either to Badger or to Kenge and Carboy like grim death, and
should have begun to be steady and systematic by this time, and
shouldn’t be in debt,  and—”

c6:p46.text:
The furniture, old-fashioned rather than old, like the house, was as
pleasantly irregular. Ada’s sleeping-room was all flowers—in chintz
and paper, in velvet, in needlework, in the brocade of two stiff
courtly chairs which stood, each attended by a little page of a stool
for greater state, on either side of the fire-place. Our sitting-room
was green and had framed and glazed upon the walls numbers of
surprising and surprised birds, staring out of pictures at a real
trout in a case, as brown and shining as if it had been served with
gravy; at the death of Captain Cook; and at the whole process of
preparing tea in China, as depicted by Chinese artists. In my room
there were oval engravings of the months—ladies haymaking in short
waists and large hats tied under the chin, for June; smooth-legged
noblemen pointing with cocked-hats to village steeples, for October.
Half-length portraits in crayons abounded all through the house, but
were so dispersed that I found the brother of a youthful officer of
mine in the china-closet and the grey old age of my pretty young
bride, with a flower in her bodice, in the breakfast-room. As
substitutes, I had four angels, of Queen Anne’s reign, taking a
complacent gentleman to heaven, in festoons, with some difficulty;
and a composition in needlework representing fruit, a kettle, and an
alphabet. All the movables, from the wardrobes to the chairs and
tables, hangings, glasses, even to the pincushions and scent-bottles
on the dressing-tables, displayed the same quaint variety. They
agreed in nothing but their perfect neatness, their display of the
whitest linen, and their storing-up, wheresoever the existence of a
drawer, small or large, rendered it possible, of quantities of
rose-leaves and sweet lavender. Such, with its illuminated windows,
softened here and there by shadows of curtains, shining out upon the
starlight night; with its light, and warmth, and comfort; with its
hospitable jingle, at a distance, of preparations for dinner; with
the face of its generous master brightening everything we saw; and
just wind enough without to sound a low accompaniment to everything
we heard, were our first impressions of Bleak House.
c6:p46.summary: Detailed description of Bleak House's furnishings in each room, establishing a warm, hospitable environment filled with quirky collections and careful comfort.

c9:p49.text:
“By my soul,” exclaimed Mr. Boythorn, suddenly firing another volley,
“that fellow is, and his father was, and his grandfather was, the
most stiff-necked, arrogant imbecile, pig-headed numskull, ever, by
some inexplicable mistake of Nature, born in any station of life but
a walking-stick’s! The whole of that family are the most solemnly
conceited and consummate blockheads! But it’s no matter; he should
not shut up my path if he were fifty baronets melted into one and
living in a hundred Chesney Wolds, one within another, like the ivory
balls in a Chinese carving. The fellow, by his agent, or secretary,
or somebody, writes to me ‘Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, presents
his compliments to Mr. Lawrence Boythorn, and has to call his
attention to the fact that the green pathway by the old
parsonage-house, now the property of Mr. Lawrence Boythorn, is Sir
Leicester’s right of way, being in fact a portion of the park of
Chesney Wold, and that Sir Leicester finds it convenient to close up
the same.’ I write to the fellow, ‘Mr. Lawrence Boythorn presents his
compliments to Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, and has to call HIS
attention to the fact that he totally denies the whole of Sir
Leicester Dedlock’s positions on every possible subject and has to
add, in reference to closing up the pathway, that he will be glad to
see the man who may undertake to do it.’ The fellow sends a most
abandoned villain with one eye to construct a gateway. I play upon
that execrable scoundrel with a fire-engine until the breath is
nearly driven out of his body. The fellow erects a gate in the night.
I chop it down and burn it in the morning. He sends his myrmidons to
come over the fence and pass and repass. I catch them in humane man
traps, fire split peas at their legs, play upon them with the
engine—resolve to free mankind from the insupportable burden of the
existence of those lurking ruffians. He brings actions for trespass;
I bring actions for trespass. He brings actions for assault and
battery; I defend them and continue to assault and batter. Ha, ha,
ha!”
c9:p49.summary: Boythorn launches an elaborate account of his escalating disputes with Sir Leicester over a right of way, detailing the volleys of letters, his theatrical retaliation with a fire engine, his destruction of gates, and the counter-actions in law, all recounted with relish and concluding with triumphant laughter.
c9:p49.best_quote: He brings actions for trespass; I bring actions for trespass. He brings actions for assault and battery; I defend them and continue to assault and batter. Ha, ha, ha!

c6:p9.text:
The notes revived in Richard and Ada a general impression that they
both had, without quite knowing how they came by it, that their
cousin Jarndyce could never bear acknowledgments for any kindness he
performed and that sooner than receive any he would resort to the
most singular expedients and evasions or would even run away. Ada
dimly remembered to have heard her mother tell, when she was a very
little child, that he had once done her an act of uncommon generosity
and that on her going to his house to thank him, he happened to see
her through a window coming to the door, and immediately escaped by
the back gate, and was not heard of for three months. This discourse
led to a great deal more on the same theme, and indeed it lasted us
all day, and we talked of scarcely anything else. If we did by any
chance diverge into another subject, we soon returned to this, and
wondered what the house would be like, and when we should get there,
and whether we should see Mr. Jarndyce as soon as we arrived or after
a delay, and what he would say to us, and what we should say to him.

“She had been a lady of a handsome figure and a noble carriage. She
never complained of the change; she never spoke to any one of being
crippled or of being in pain, but day by day she tried to walk upon
the terrace, and with the help of the stone balustrade, went up and
down, up and down, up and down, in sun and shadow, with greater
difficulty every day. At last, one afternoon her husband (to whom she
had never, on any persuasion, opened her lips since that night),
standing at the great south window, saw her drop upon the pavement.
He hastened down to raise her, but she repulsed him as he bent over
her, and looking at him fixedly and coldly, said, ‘I will die here
where I have walked. And I will walk here, though I am in my grave. I
will walk here until the pride of this house is humbled. And when
calamity or when disgrace is coming to it, let the Dedlocks listen
for my step!’”

c56:p51.text:
“Now, Mr. Jarndyce”—Mr. Bucket has read his face with the greatest
attention all along—“I speak to you as a gentleman of a humane
heart, and under such pressing circumstances as don’t often happen.
If ever delay was dangerous, it’s dangerous now; and if ever you
couldn’t afterwards forgive yourself for causing it, this is the
time. Eight or ten hours, worth, as I tell you, a hundred pound
apiece at least, have been lost since Lady Dedlock disappeared. I am
charged to find her. I am Inspector Bucket. Besides all the rest
that’s heavy on her, she has upon her, as she believes, suspicion of
murder. If I follow her alone, she, being in ignorance of what Sir
Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, has communicated to me, may be driven to
desperation. But if I follow her in company with a young lady,
answering to the description of a young lady that she has a
tenderness for—I ask no question, and I say no more than that—she
will give me credit for being friendly. Let me come up with her and
be able to have the hold upon her of putting that young lady for’ard,
and I’ll save her and prevail with her if she is alive. Let me come
up with her alone—a hard matter—and I’ll do my best, but I don’t
answer for what the best may be. Time flies; it’s getting on for one

a thousand pound now instead of a hundred.”
c56:p51.summary: Mr. Bucket makes a compelling case to Mr. Jarndyce: without Esther, Lady Dedlock may despair and take her own life; with Esther's presence, Lady Dedlock may trust him and be saved. He emphasizes that time is critical and frames the request as a matter of life and death.
c56:p51.best_quote: If I follow her alone, she, being in ignorance of what Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, has communicated to me, may be driven to desperation. But if I follow her in company with a young lady, answering to the description of a young lady that she has a tenderness for—I ask no question, and I say no more than that—she will give me credit for being friendly.

c64:p27.text:
We went out of the porch and he showed me written over it, Bleak
House.
c64:p27.summary: The house is named Bleak House—the same name as Jarndyce's own home.
